citation.title: Confidence Intervals for Linear Unbiased Estimators under Constrained Dependence

standing_assumptions:
The article is Electronic Journal of Statistics 12 (2018) 2238–2252. Printed page = PDF page + 2237 (printed p. 2240 is PDF p. 3). Everything quoted from the article was read from the page images (staged/pages/p-NN.png, re-rendered at 200 dpi for the formulas).
(S1) Graph and dependency graph. p. 2240 (PDF p. 3): "Consider a simple graph $\mathcal G = (\mathcal V, \mathcal E)$ with no parallel edges or self-loops. Let $|\mathcal V| = N$. Associated with each vertex $i \in \mathcal V$ is a random variable $Y_i$, and $\mathcal G$ characterizes probabilistic dependencies in the outcomes [e.g., 3]." "Definition 1 (Dependency graph). $\mathcal G$ is a dependency graph if for all disjoint sets $\mathcal V_1, \mathcal V_2 \subset \mathcal V$ with no edge in $\mathcal E$ connecting a vertex in $\mathcal V_1$ to a vertex in $\mathcal V_2$, the set $\{Y_i : i \in \mathcal V_1\}$ is independent from the set $\{Y_j : j \in \mathcal V_2\}$."
(S2) Observation. p. 2240 (PDF p. 3): "Suppose $\mathcal G$ is a dependency graph and we observe a subset $\mathcal V_S \subseteq \mathcal V$, where $|\mathcal V_S| = n$. Label these observed vertices $1, \ldots, n$, and label the unobserved vertices in $\mathcal V \setminus \mathcal V_S$ arbitrarily by $n+1, \ldots, N$. For each $i \in \mathcal V_S$, we observe the outcomes $Y_1, \ldots, Y_n$, a fixed vector of coefficients $\theta = \theta_1, \ldots, \theta_n$, and the degrees $d_i = |\{j : \{i,j\} \in \mathcal E\}|$ for each $i \in \mathcal V_S$." "Definition 2 (Induced subgraph). For a set of vertices $\mathcal V_S \subseteq \mathcal V$, the induced subgraph in $\mathcal G$ is $\mathcal G_S = (\mathcal V_S, \mathcal E_S)$, where $\mathcal E_S = \{\{i,j\} : i \in \mathcal V_S,\ j \in \mathcal V_S,\ \text{and } \{i,j\} \in \mathcal E\}$." "Let $\mathcal G_S = (\mathcal V_S, \mathcal E_S)$ be the induced subgraph of the observed vertices $\mathcal V_S$. It follows that $\mathcal G_S$ is also a dependency graph. Let $\mathcal G_R = (\mathcal V_S, \mathcal E_R)$ be a subgraph of $\mathcal G_S$, consisting of all the observed vertices in $\mathcal V_S$, and a subset of the edges in $\mathcal E_S$." "Assumption 1 (Observed data). We observe the random outcomes $Y_1, \ldots, Y_n$, the fixed degrees $d_1, \ldots, d_n$, the fixed coefficients $\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_n$, and the fixed recruitment graph $\mathcal G_R$." "Let $Y = (Y_1, \ldots, Y_n)$, $d = (d_1, \ldots, d_n)$, and denote the observed data as $Z = (Y, d, \theta, \mathcal G_R)$."
(S3) Estimator and target. p. 2240 (PDF p. 3): "Definition 3 (Linear unbiased estimator (LUE)). An estimator $\hat\beta$ is a linear unbiased estimator (LUE) of $\beta$ if $\hat\beta = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i \in \mathcal V_S} \theta_i Y_i$ where $\mathrm{E}[\hat\beta] = \beta$." p. 2241 (PDF p. 4): "In what follows, we wish to conduct inference on $\beta$ given $Z$. We proceed by constructing conservative estimators of $\mathrm{var}(\hat\beta) = \frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i \in \mathcal V_S}^{n}\sum_{j \in \mathcal V_S}^{n} \theta_i\theta_j\,\mathrm{cov}(Y_i, Y_j)$."
(S4) Compatible adjacency matrices. p. 2241 (PDF p. 4): "We consider a class of variance estimators that depend on knowledge of $\mathcal G_S$, whose structure is represented by an $n \times n$ binary symmetric zero-diagonal adjacency matrix in which rows and columns are ordered by the indices $1, \ldots, n$ of the vertices in $\mathcal V_S$." "Definition 4 (Compatibility). The $n \times n$ binary symmetric adjacency matrix $A$ is compatible with the observed data $Z$ if for each $\{i,j\} \in \mathcal E_R$, $A_{ij} = A_{ji} = 1$, and for each $i \in \mathcal V_S$, $\sum_{j \in \mathcal V_S} A_{ij} \le d_i$." "The last condition in Definition 4 requires that the degree of $i$ in the subgraph $\mathcal G_S$ not be greater than its degree in the full graph $\mathcal G$. Let $A^{\mathcal O} = \{A^{\mathcal O}_{ij}\}$ be the true $n \times n$ adjacency matrix of $\mathcal G_S$, where $A^{\mathcal O}_{ij} = 1$ if $\{i,j\} \in \mathcal E_S$ for $i, j \in \mathcal V_S$ and 0 otherwise. Let $\mathcal A(Z) = \{A : A \text{ is compatible with } Z\}$ in the sense of Definition 4; it is clear that $A^{\mathcal O} \in \mathcal A(Z)$." "Definition 5 (Oracle estimator). For a family of variance estimators $\widehat V(A;Z)$ defined for $A \in \mathcal A(Z)$, the oracle estimator is $\widehat V(A^{\mathcal O};Z)$." "For a variance estimator $\widehat V(A;Z)$, define the set $\mathcal A^m = \{A \in \mathcal A(Z) : \widehat V(A;Z) \text{ is maximized}\}$." "Definition 6 (Maximal compatible estimator). Let $A^m \in \mathcal A^m$. The maximal compatible estimator is $\widehat V(A^m;Z)$."
(S5) Asymptotic scaling. p. 2242 (PDF p. 5): "Assumption 2 (Asymptotic scaling). Consider the sequence $(\mathcal G, Z)_n$ of nested graphs $\mathcal G$ and observed data $Z = (\mathcal G_R, Y, d)$, where $\mathcal G_R = (\mathcal V_S, \mathcal E_R)$, $|\mathcal V_S| = n$, and $|\mathcal V| = N_n \ge n$. Assume there exist finite, positive constants $c_1$, $c_2$ such that for every element $(\mathcal G, Z)_n$, $\Pr(|\theta_i Y_i - \beta| > c_1) = 0, \forall i \in \mathcal V_S$ (bounded outcome values) and $\sum_{j \in \mathcal V_S} A^{\mathcal O}_{ij} \le c_2, \forall i \in \mathcal V_S$ (bounded degrees in dependency graph). Further assume there exists a finite, positive constant $c_3$ such that $\lim_{n\to\infty} n\,\mathrm{var}(\hat\beta) = c_3$ (nondegenerate limiting variance). Finally, assume $c_4$ is a finite positive constant such that $|\theta_i| < c_4$."
(S6) General estimator. p. 2242 (PDF p. 5): "Define the plug-in sample variance $\hat\sigma_\theta^2 = n^{-1}\sum_{i \in \mathcal V_S}(\theta_i Y_i - \hat\beta)^2$, and the estimator $\widehat V_1(A;Z) = \frac{1}{n^2}\left[n\hat\sigma_\theta^2 + \sum_{i \in \mathcal V_S}\sum_{j \in \mathcal V_S} A_{ij}(\theta_i Y_i - \hat\beta)(\theta_j Y_j - \hat\beta)\right]$. (3.1)" p. 2244 (PDF p. 7): "Let $\mathcal A_1^m = \{A \in \mathcal A(Z) : \widehat V_1(A;Z) \text{ is maximized}\}$ be the set of compatible adjacency matrices that maximize $\widehat V_1(A;Z)$. Let $\Theta = \mathrm{diag}(\theta)$ be the $n \times n$ matrix with $\Theta_{ii} = \theta_i$ and $\Theta_{ij} = 0$ for $i \ne j$."
(S7) Homoskedastic estimators. p. 2246 (PDF p. 9): "Assumption 3 (Homoskedasticity). $\mathrm{var}(\theta_i Y_i) = \mathrm{var}(\theta_j Y_j), \forall i, j \in \mathcal V$." "A bound that is relatively computationally simple to compute can be derived by noting that when $\mathrm{var}(\theta_i Y_i) = \sigma_\theta^2$, $\mathrm{cov}(\theta_i Y_i, \theta_j Y_j) \le \sigma_\theta^2 A^{\mathcal O}_{ij}$. Define the estimator $\widehat V_2(A;Z) = \frac{\hat\sigma_\theta^2}{n}\left[1 + \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i \in \mathcal V_S}\sum_{j \in \mathcal V_S} A_{ij}\right]$. (3.7)" "Define $\mathcal A_2^m = \{A \in \mathcal A(Z) : \widehat V_2(A;Z) \text{ is maximized}\}$, and let $A^m \in \mathcal A_2^m$." pp. 2246–2247 (PDF pp. 9–10): "For $i \in \mathcal V_S$, let $d_i' = \min\{d_i, n-1\}$ be the degree of $i$ in $\mathcal G$, truncated at $n-1$. Let $\widehat V_2'(Z) = \frac{\hat\sigma_\theta^2}{n}\left[1 + \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i \in \mathcal V_S} d_i'\right]$. (3.9)"
(S8) Degree bounds in place of degrees. p. 2248 (PDF p. 11): "Alternatively, we may not have full knowledge of the degrees $d = (d_1, \ldots, d_n)$, and instead have only an upper bound $d_i^*$ for each $d_i$, or a global upper bound $d_i \le d^*$ for all $i = 1, \ldots, n$. Conservative variance estimation in both of these cases can be achieved (by substituting $d_i^*$ or $d^*$ for $d_i$) with no change to the programs (3.5) and (3.8) or to the asymptotic results given here. When no information about $\mathcal G_R$ or the degrees $d$ is available, setting every $d_i = d^* = n-1$ delivers a maximally conservative upper bound."
(S9) Audit notation, not in the paper (from the validators' derivations and the from-scratch check of the correction). $X_i = \theta_i Y_i$; $\mu_i = \mathrm{E}[X_i]$; $\delta_i = \mu_i - \beta$ (so $\sum_i \delta_i = 0$ by Definition 3, but no $\delta_i$ need be 0); $u_i = X_i - \mu_i$; $e_i = X_i - \hat\beta$; $C$ is the $n \times n$ covariance matrix of $(X_1, \ldots, X_n)$; $S = I + A^{\mathcal O}$; $b_n = \frac{1}{n}\delta^{\mathsf T}(I + A^{\mathcal O})\delta = \frac{1}{n}\left[\sum_i \delta_i^2 + \sum_i\sum_j A^{\mathcal O}_{ij}\delta_i\delta_j\right]$; for a symmetric $n \times n$ matrix $M$, $\widehat V_M = \frac{1}{n^2}e^{\mathsf T}Me$, so that $\widehat V_1(A;Z) = \widehat V_{I+A}$; for an adjacency matrix $A$, $d_i^A = \sum_j A_{ij}$ and $D_A = \mathrm{diag}(d_i^A)$; $D' = \mathrm{diag}(d_i')$. By Definition 1, $C_{ij} = 0$ whenever $i \ne j$ and $A^{\mathcal O}_{ij} = 0$, so $n\,\mathrm{var}(\hat\beta) = \frac{1}{n}\mathrm{tr}\{(I + A^{\mathcal O})C\}$.
(S10) Reading conventions (for the formalizer; conventions, not quotations). (a) At each $n$ there is one probability space carrying the outcomes; $\mathrm{E}$, $\mathrm{var}$, $\mathrm{cov}$, $\Pr$ refer to their joint law. The graphs, the degrees $d_i$ and the coefficients $\theta_i$ are non-random; they and $\beta = \mathrm{E}[\hat\beta]$ may depend on $n$ (the regression weights of Section 2 do). (b) The constants $c_1, \ldots, c_4$ of Assumption 2 do not depend on $n$, and its conditions hold for every $n$ and every $i \in \mathcal V_S$. (c) "$\lim_{n\to\infty}\Pr(\cdot > \epsilon) = 0$ for any $\epsilon > 0$" is a statement about the sequence indexed by $n$. (d) "will have (at least) $100(1-\alpha)\%$ coverage for $\beta$ in large $n$" is read as: the limit (limit inferior) of $\Pr(|\hat\beta - \beta| \le z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\widehat V})$ equals (is at least) $1 - \alpha$, for $0 < \alpha < 1$, with $z_{1-\alpha/2} = \Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha/2)$. The printed interval is undefined when $\widehat V < 0$, which can happen for $\widehat V_1$; the corrected statements use $\max\{\widehat V, 0\}$. (e) Double sums over $i, j \in \mathcal V_S$ are over ordered pairs. (f) In (3.5), $\Theta Y - \hat\beta$ is the vector with entries $\theta_i Y_i - \hat\beta$, $1$ is the vector of ones, and $\preceq$, $\succeq$ are element-wise $\le$, $\ge$ (the print says "less-than"; P011-N001). (g) Assumption 3 is used only for $i, j \in \mathcal V_S$ (P011-N001); the common variance, which may depend on $n$, is written $\sigma_\theta^2$ in the paper and $\sigma_n^2$ in the corrected statements. (h) "Valid constraints" means $\mathcal E_R \subseteq \mathcal E_S$ and $d_i \ge \sum_j A^{\mathcal O}_{ij}$ for every $i \in \mathcal V_S$ (true degrees in $\mathcal G$, or upper bounds on them as in (S8)), which gives $A^{\mathcal O} \in \mathcal A(Z)$. (i) In Corollaries 1 and 3, $A^m \in \mathcal A_1^m$; in Lemma 1 and Corollaries 2 and 4, $A^m \in \mathcal A_2^m$.
Scope of the list. Targets come from two sources. (1) Headline claims P011-H1 to P011-H7 are mathematical and are targets (H1 and H4 are false as printed and appear as results touched by P011-E001; H2, H3, H5, H6 and the formal part of H7 appear as headline results). P011-H8 (the R package implements the method) is a statement about software and is not a target. (2) Confirmed errors whose correction changes a mathematical statement, a formula or a proof step: P011-E001 (Critical; targets T1–T10, T31–T33, with the corrected statements taken from the from-scratch check runs/P011/correction-recheck/recheck.json, as NOTES-FOR-AGENTS.md directs), P011-E004 (Moderate; T11, T12, T34), P011-E002 (Moderate; T13, T14, T30), P011-N006 (Moderate; an interpretive finding about the package vignette and README that rests on an exact counterexample; T15, T16, T35), and the Minor errors P011-E003 (T17, T18), P011-E005 (T19, T20), P011-E006 (T21), P011-E007 (T22, T23), P011-N001 (T24) and P011-E015 (T25, T26; the package's variance helpers use divisor $n-1$ where the paper's formulas (3.1), (3.7), (3.9) use $n$, a wrong constant relative to the printed formulas). Not targets: P011-E009 and P011-N007 (misprinted words), P011-N002 (bibliography), P011-E011, P011-E013 and P011-E014 (the package stops with an error or does not check the solver status: no formula or statement to correct), P011-E012 (the help page and vignette name estimator (3.9) where the code returns (3.7) at the optimized graph; both formulas and Lemma 1, which relates them, are correct as printed and are target T28, so there is no mathematical statement to correct), P011-E010 (out of scope), P011-E008 (clarity note), P011-N003 and P011-N008 (undetermined), P011-N004 and P011-N005 (not confirmed).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Proof of Proposition 2, the convergence display as printed (with $< \epsilon$)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed statement refuted, p. 2246] "$\lim_{n\to\infty}\Pr(|n\widehat V_2^*(A^{\mathcal O};Z) - n\,\mathrm{var}(\hat\beta)| < \epsilon) = 0$."
[Counterexample, from the validator] Let $Y_1, Y_2, \ldots$ be independent with $\Pr(Y_i = 1) = \Pr(Y_i = -1) = 1/2$, $\theta_i = 1$, and for every $n$ the edgeless graph on $\{1, \ldots, n\}$ with every vertex observed, $\mathcal E_R = \emptyset$, $A^{\mathcal O} = 0$, $d_i = 0$. Then $\beta = 0$, $\mathrm{E}[\theta_iY_i] = \beta$ for every $i$, $|\theta_iY_i - \beta| = 1$, $\mathrm{var}(\theta_iY_i) = 1$ for every $i$, and $n\,\mathrm{var}(\hat\beta) = 1$: Assumptions 2 and 3 hold ($c_1 = 1$, $c_2 = 1$, $c_3 = 1$, $c_4 = 2$).
(a) $n\widehat V_2^*(A^{\mathcal O};Z) = \hat\sigma_\theta^2 = 1 - \hat\beta^2$, so $|n\widehat V_2^*(A^{\mathcal O};Z) - n\,\mathrm{var}(\hat\beta)| = \hat\beta^2$.
(b) $\mathrm{E}[\hat\beta^2] = 1/n$, so for every $\epsilon > 0$: $\Pr(|n\widehat V_2^*(A^{\mathcal O};Z) - n\,\mathrm{var}(\hat\beta)| < \epsilon) \ge 1 - \frac{1}{n\epsilon} \to 1$, not 0.
(c) Exact values at $\epsilon = 1/2$: the probability is $1/2$ at $n = 2$, $7/8$ at $n = 4$ and $32631/32768$ at $n = 16$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The auxiliary estimator of the printed proof: P011-T34 (with $A^{\mathcal O} = 0$ the correlation term is absent). $\hat\sigma_\theta^2 = \frac1n\sum_i(Y_i - \hat\beta)^2$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: (1) $\frac1n\sum_i(Y_i - \hat\beta)^2 = \frac1n\sum_iY_i^2 - \hat\beta^2 = 1 - \hat\beta^2$. (2) $\mathrm{E}[\hat\beta^2] = \mathrm{var}(\hat\beta) = 1/n$. (3) Markov's inequality: $\Pr(\hat\beta^2 \ge \epsilon) \le \frac{1}{n\epsilon}$. (4) For (c): with $S_n = \sum_iY_i$, the event is $S_n^2 < n^2/2$.
canonical_claim.note: Batch verdict for P011-E005 (work/derivations.md). The exact values in (c) are from the enumeration of the validator of P011-E004 (runs/P011/validate/P011-E004/v1/artifact/check_exact.out, homogeneous-means case, which has the same error distribution). The unit means are equal here, so this refutes the printed sign independently of P011-E004.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Proof of Proposition 2, the correlations of the auxiliary estimator, with the pair index restored
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Assumption 3, (3.7), Definition 1: standing assumptions. The printed proof: P011-T34. In (i) the double sum is over ordered pairs and $A^{\mathcal O}_{ii} = 0$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: (1) $n\,\mathrm{var}(\hat\beta) = \frac1n\left[\sum_i\mathrm{var}(X_i) + \sum_{i \ne j}\mathrm{cov}(X_i, X_j)\right]$ and $\mathrm{cov}(X_i, X_j) = 0$ for $i \ne j$ with $A^{\mathcal O}_{ij} = 0$. (2) The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality with equal variances gives $\mathrm{cov}(X_i, X_j) \le \sigma_\theta^2$. (3) $\hat\sigma_\theta^2 \ge 0$ and $A^{\mathcal O}_{ij} \ge 0$. (4) In (iii): $\frac13\left(3 + 2\left(\tfrac35 + \tfrac45\right)\right) = \frac{29}{15}$.
canonical_claim.note: Batch verdict for P011-E006. The validator notes that a degree-weighted neighbour average rho_i = (sum_j A^O_ij rho_ij)/(sum_j A^O_ij) would reproduce the double sum, but the paper gives no such definition; the instance (iii) shows only that rho_i cannot be the correlation of unit i with each of its neighbours. Restoring the index does not establish the consistency asserted next in the proof (P011-E004).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The decision variables of program (3.6), corrected, and the equivalence of (3.5) and (3.6)
canonical_claim.location: Sentence defining the decision variables: p. 2244 (PDF p. 7), last paragraph; program (3.6): p. 2245 (PDF p. 8)
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Programs (3.5), (3.6), (3.8) as printed: P011-T27. $\Theta = \mathrm{diag}(\theta)$, (3.1), $\mathcal A_1^m$: standing assumptions (S6). $A_R$ is the adjacency matrix of $\mathcal G_R$. The paper calls $\hat v_{ij}$ "the $ij$th element of the sample covariance matrix" without defining it; (3.5) fixes it as the product of centred weighted outcomes.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: (1) For symmetric zero-diagonal $A$ and any vector $r$: $r^{\mathsf T}Ar = \sum_{i \ne j}A_{ij}r_ir_j = 2\sum_{i<j}A_{ij}r_ir_j$. (2) $n^2\widehat V_1(A;Z) = n\hat\sigma_\theta^2 + r^{\mathsf T}Ar$ with $r_i = \theta_iY_i - \hat\beta$.
canonical_claim.note: Batch verdict for P011-E007: the printed "if" condition fixes the optimization variables from the data; program (3.6) itself and the staged implementation use the edge-selection indicator. Repair cost: none; nothing depends on the printed sentence.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The decision variables of program (3.6), as printed
canonical_claim.location: p. 2244 (PDF p. 7), last paragraph; program (3.6): p. 2245 (PDF p. 8)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed statement refuted, p. 2244] "Let $\hat v_{ij}$ be the $ij$th element of the sample covariance matrix with $i = 1, ..., n$ and $j = 1, ..., n$. Since the sample covariance matrix is symmetric, we can focus on its upper triangular part and use the decision variable $a_{ij} = 1$ if $\hat v_{ij} \ne 0$, and 0 otherwise, for each $i < j$."
[Counterexample, from the validator] $n = 3$, $\theta_i = 1$, $Y = (-2, \tfrac12, \tfrac32)$, so $\hat\beta = 0$ and the centred weighted outcomes are $(-2, \tfrac12, \tfrac32)$; degree bounds $d = (1, 1, 1)$; no mandatory edges ($\mathcal E_R = \emptyset$).
(a) $\hat v_{12} = -1$, $\hat v_{13} = -3$, $\hat v_{23} = \tfrac34$, all nonzero; the printed rule therefore sets $a_{12} = a_{13} = a_{23} = 1$.
(b) These values give every vertex degree 2, which violates the constraints $\sum_{j<i}a_{ji} + \sum_{j>i}a_{ij} \le d_i = 1$ of (3.6): the printed "decision variables" are not feasible for the program they are said to define.
(c) The optimum of (3.6) on these data is $\tfrac34$, attained only by $a_{23} = 1$, $a_{12} = a_{13} = 0$.
(d) The printed rule can also contradict $A \succeq A_R$: an edge $\{i,j\} \in \mathcal E_R$ with $\hat v_{ij} = 0$ gets $a_{ij} = 0$. An instance (constructed here to illustrate the validator's remark): $Y = (0, 1, -1)$, $\theta_i = 1$, $\hat\beta = 0$, $\mathcal E_R = \{\{1,2\}\}$, where $\hat v_{12} = 0$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Program (3.6) as printed: P011-T27. $\hat v_{ij} = (\theta_iY_i - \hat\beta)(\theta_jY_j - \hat\beta)$, as (3.5) requires.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: The feasible points of (3.6) for $d = (1, 1, 1)$ are the empty graph and the three single edges, with objective values $0, -1, -3, \tfrac34$.
canonical_claim.note: Batch verdict for P011-E007, evidence type exact counterexample (work/math_checks.py, work/math_results.json key E007). Part (d) states the validator's second remark ("fail to include a mandatory edge with zero coefficient"); the three-unit instance for it was written when these targets were fixed and is not in the validator's files.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Notation corrected in Assumption 2, program (3.5), Assumption 3 and Section 3.2: the observed data $Z$, the relation $\preceq$, the index set of Assumption 3, and the edge set $\mathcal E_S$
canonical_claim.location: Assumption 2: p. 2242 (PDF p. 5); program (3.5): p. 2244 (PDF p. 7); Assumption 3 and the last paragraph: p. 2246 (PDF p. 9); Discussion: p. 2248 (PDF p. 11)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Corrected text, from the validator] (a) In Assumption 2 and in the Discussion the observed data are $Z = (Y, d, \theta, \mathcal G_R)$, as defined after Assumption 1 on p. 2240 (the print has $Z = (\mathcal G_R, Y, d)$ on p. 2242 and $Z = (Y, d, \mathcal G_R)$ on p. 2248, omitting $\theta$). (b) After program (3.5): "$\preceq$ denotes the element-wise 'less-than-or-equal-to' relation" (the print has "less-than"). (c) Assumption 3 (Homoskedasticity): $\mathrm{var}(\theta_iY_i) = \mathrm{var}(\theta_jY_j), \forall i, j \in \mathcal V_S$ (the print has $\forall i, j \in \mathcal V$). (d) On p. 2246, "the maximum number of edges that can be in $\mathcal E_S$" (the print has a roman $\mathrm E_S$).
[Formal content]
(i) With $\preceq$ read as element-wise $\le$ and $\succeq$ as element-wise $\ge$, the feasible set of (3.5) and of (3.8), $\{A \text{ binary symmetric zero-diagonal} : A1 \preceq d,\ A \succeq A_R\}$, is exactly $\mathcal A(Z)$ of Definition 4, and it contains $A^{\mathcal O}$ (valid constraints).
(ii) Assumption 3 as corrected is a condition on the $n$ random variables $\theta_1Y_1, \ldots, \theta_nY_n$; the coefficients $\theta_i$ are defined only for $i \in \mathcal V_S = \{1, \ldots, n\}$, while $\mathcal V = \{1, \ldots, N\}$ with $N \ge n$. The bound $\mathrm{cov}(\theta_iY_i, \theta_jY_j) \le \sigma_\theta^2A^{\mathcal O}_{ij}$ for $i \ne j$ in $\mathcal V_S$, the estimators (3.7) and (3.9), Proposition 2, Lemma 1 and Corollaries 2 and 4 involve only $i, j \in \mathcal V_S$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Definition 4, $\mathcal A(Z)$, Assumptions 1–3 as printed: standing assumptions (S2), (S4), (S5), (S7). Program (3.5) as printed: P011-T27. $A_R$ is the adjacency matrix of $\mathcal G_R$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: (1) $(A1)_i = \sum_{j \in \mathcal V_S}A_{ij}$, so $A1 \le d$ element-wise is the degree condition of Definition 4; $A \ge A_R$ element-wise for binary symmetric $A$ is $A_{ij} = A_{ji} = 1$ for each $\{i,j\} \in \mathcal E_R$. (2) $A^{\mathcal O} \ge A_R$ because $\mathcal E_R \subseteq \mathcal E_S$, and $\sum_jA^{\mathcal O}_{ij} \le d_i$ because the degree of $i$ in $\mathcal G_S$ is at most its degree in $\mathcal G$.
canonical_claim.note: Batch verdict for P011-N001, confirmed in part: items (a), (e), (f), (g) of the candidate are confirmed and are the four corrections above; items (b), (c), (d), (h) (two local meanings of Theta, a redundant upper limit on a sum, the scalar subtracted from a vector in (3.5), and A^m, A for A_2^m, A(Z) in Lemma 1 and its proof) are not errors. No result depends on these misprints. A consequence of (b), given for the formalizer and not taken from the validator: under the printed strict reading, sum_j A_ij < d_i for every i, the matrix A^O would be infeasible whenever some observed vertex has all its neighbours observed (as in P011-T1 and P011-T2, where the feasible set would be empty), contrary to Definition 4 and to "it is clear that A^O is in A(Z)" on p. 2241.
